title: After the Permanent Plan: Post-Permanency Reviews
statement: After a permanent plan is chosen, the court holds a review every six months for as long as the case stays open.
steps: Two sources differ. Booklet p.18: 'the court will have a hearing every six months'. WIC 366.3(d)(1): status 'reviewed at least every six months' but review 'may be conducted by the court or an appropriate local agency'; court must do it when '12 months since a review was conducted by the court' or on a parent's request. Review by the court is always required when rights were ended and the child is placed for adoption.
fix: After a permanent plan is chosen, the child's case is reviewed at least every six months while the case stays open. Most reviews are in court. Some can be done by a county review panel, but the judge must do a review at least once a year. You can ask for the judge to do it.

title: Appeals and Writs: Challenging a Decision
statement: If you believe the judge made a legal mistake, you can ask a higher court to review the decision.
source_says: A judgment in a proceeding under Section 300 may be appealed in the same manner as any final judgment
steps: Opened public.law WIC 395, read (a)(1).

title: Appeals and Writs: Challenging a Decision
statement: For most orders you have 60 days to file a notice of appeal.
source_says: a notice of appeal must be filed within 60 days after the rendition of the judgment
steps: Opened rule 8.406 at the entry's own link; read (a). Exceptions seen: referee orders run from when the order becomes final; 30 days for transfer orders (not dependency).

title: Appeals and Writs: Challenging a Decision
statement: The first order you can appeal is usually the disposition order.
source_says: The dispositional order is the "judgment" referred to in section 395, and all subsequent orders are appealable.
steps: WIC 395 and rule 8.406 do not name the disposition order. Searched for the case law; opened In re S.B. on scocal.stanford.edu. Rule 5.590(a) also has the court advise of appeal rights 'after making its disposition order'.

title: Appeals and Writs: Challenging a Decision
statement: Problems with the jurisdiction hearing are raised in that appeal.
source_says: review of findings is normally obtained by appeal from the ensuing judgment or order
steps: Opened In re S.B. on scocal.stanford.edu. The opinion states the general rule for findings; it does not use the word 'jurisdictional' in that sentence.

title: Appeals and Writs: Challenging a Decision
statement: If you cannot afford a lawyer for the appeal, one is appointed for you at no cost.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court rule 8.403(b)(2); rule 5.590(a)(3)
steps: Two rules read differently. Rule 8.403(b)(2): 'The reviewing court may appoint counsel to represent an indigent child, parent, or guardian.' Rule 5.590(a)(3): 'The right of an indigent appellant to have counsel appointed by the reviewing court'. Neither rule mentions cost. The dogbook PDF would not open (client error).
fix: If you cannot afford a lawyer for the appeal, you can ask the appeals court to give you one. Ask your trial lawyer how to do this.

title: Fee Waiver (FW-001): How to Waive Court Filing Fees
statement: How to get your court filing fees waived if you cannot afford them
source_says: There shall be no fee for filing a petition under this chapter nor shall any fees be charged by any public officer

Also opened FW-001-INFO: it lists civil, family law, and guardianship or conservatorship cases, not juvenile cases. The page never tells a dependency parent that juvenile court does not charge a fee to file a petition.
fix: Juvenile dependency court does not charge a fee to file a petition. You may need a fee waiver in other courts, like family court or a guardianship case. This page tells you how to ask.

steps: Opened rule 5.534(a). The judge may grant standing to take part as a party.

title: Educational Rights Holder (JV-535)
statement: One reason is a parent who does not respond to the school or attend school meetings.

steps: Opened every cited source plus rule 5.649, WIC 319 and form JV-535. None names 'not responding to the school' or 'not attending meetings' as a reason. WIC 361(a) and rule 5.649 allow a limit only when needed to protect the child. WIC 319(j) allows a temporary limit when the parent is unavailable, unable, or unwilling, the court made diligent efforts to find the parent, and the child's needs cannot be met otherwise.
fix: The judge can limit these rights only when it is needed to protect the child. Early in a case, the judge can do it for a short time if a parent cannot be found or is not able or willing to make school decisions.

title: Educational Rights Holder (JV-535)
